orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, still telling her story to Lockwood. It is the day after Catherine's funeral, in late March 1784 by the usual scholarly dating, and Nelly is at Thrushcross Grange with the newborn baby. For a long stretch Nelly lets someone else talk, repeating a visitor's account in her own words, and the later pages move quickly through the following months.

notes.t: made the last of our fine days
notes.g: Was the last of our good-weather days.

notes.n: Primroses are pale yellow wild flowers; crocuses are small cup-shaped flowers that come up in early spring.

notes.g: Small brown songbirds of open country.
notes.n: Skylarks are famous for singing while hovering high over fields and moors.

notes.g: Struck and blackened by the frost.
Turning it into a room for the baby.

notes.t: the moaning doll of a child
notes.n: Catherine's newborn daughter, born the night her mother died (Chapter XVI).

notes.m: Not dizziness. 'Giddy' meant frivolous and light-headed.

notes.g: Except where I ran so fast I seemed to fly.
Tell the coachman to get the horses and carriage ready.
The nearby village, with the church, the doctor and the lawyer.
The visitor is Isabella, Edgar's sister, who ran off and married Heathcliff.
notes.n: Careful: in Chapters I to III 'Mrs. Heathcliff' was the young widow Lockwood met at the Heights. Nelly's story is set many years earlier, so here the name means Isabella.

notes.g: In no situation to laugh about.

notes.t: befitting her age more than her position
notes.g: Suited to a young girl rather than a married woman.
notes.n: A respectable wife would normally wear a cap and cover her neck and shoulders. Isabella is still very young.

notes.g: A dress with a low neckline.
Clung to her because it was soaked.

notes.t: a frame hardly able to support itself
notes.g: A body almost too tired to stand.

notes.n: The hearth is the stone floor of the fireplace and the area just in front of it.
'Nelly' is the pet form. Isabella, as a lady, calls her Ellen.

notes.g: The newborn daughter of Catherine, who has just died.
notes.n: In this chapter, 'Catherine' almost always means the dead mother.

notes.g: We separated without making up our quarrel.
notes.n: Catherine and Isabella fell out over Heathcliff in Chapter X, before Isabella eloped.
She can hardly bear to say his name.

notes.g: The iron rod for stirring the fire.
Her ring finger, where her wedding ring was.

notes.m: Stronger than modern playful teasing: it meant to harass or plague.
Not taking him to court. To 'sue for' something meant to plead for it.

notes.t: he was out of the way
notes.n: Here 'he' is probably Edgar, whom she knows is in bed.

notes.t: Earnshaw is not his match in strength
notes.g: Hindley isn't as strong as Heathcliff.
notes.n: In this chapter 'Earnshaw' and 'Mr. Earnshaw' mean Hindley, Catherine's brother. Isabella lives in his house with Heathcliff.

notes.g: Nelly's old habit from Isabella's girlhood.
notes.n: Strictly she is now a married woman, Mrs. Heathcliff.

notes.t: sadly out of place under this roof
notes.g: Very wrong in a house in mourning.

notes.n: 'Condition' could mean the state of your health or your circumstances in general.

notes.t: committed it to a servant’s care
notes.g: Handed the baby to a servant.
The dislike he felt from the start.

notes.m: 'Perverted' just meant warped or turned the wrong way. No sexual sense.

notes.t: would that he could be blotted out
notes.g: I wish he could be wiped out.

notes.t: from this to his dying day
notes.g: From now until the day he dies.
Isabella Linton, Edgar's sister, now Heathcliff's wife.
notes.n: She eloped with Heathcliff in Chapter XII and wrote to Nelly from the Heights in Chapter XIII.

notes.t: dashing the water from her lashes
notes.g: Brushing the tears from her eyelashes.
So high that it overcame his cold, planned cruelty.

notes.t: Pulling out the nerves with red hot pincers requires more coolness than knocking on the head
notes.g: Slow torture takes more self-control than a quick blow.
notes.n: Isabella means Heathcliff usually prefers slow, careful cruelty. She made him angry enough to lose control.

notes.m: 'Signal' here is an adjective meaning remarkable, not a sign or message.

notes.t: Mr. Earnshaw should have been at the funeral
notes.g: Hindley was invited to his sister Catherine's funeral but never came.
notes.n: See the end of Chapter XVI.

notes.g: So depressed he might kill himself.

notes.t: as fit for the church as for a dance
Whether the angels have fed him, or his kin beneath
notes.g: Whether angels or his relatives in hell have been feeding him.
notes.n: A bitter joke on Bible stories where God feeds his prophets in the wilderness, as an angel feeds Elijah (1 Kings 19). 'His kin beneath' are devils.
Methodism, a newer movement in the 1700s, was known for emotional, fervent prayer, quite unlike calm Church of England services.
Echoes the burial service: 'earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust'.

notes.t: curiously confounded with his own black father
notes.g: Strangely mixed up with the devil, whom she calls his father.

notes.n: 'Orisons' is an old literary word for prayers.

notes.g: Thrushcross Grange, the Lintons' house, where Nelly and Edgar live.

notes.t: send for a constable, and give him into custody
notes.g: Call the parish constable and have him arrested.
notes.n: There was no police force yet. Each parish had a part-time constable to keep order.

notes.t: this season of deliverance from degrading oppression
notes.g: This time of freedom from his bullying.
The old, sour, strictly religious servant at Wuthering Heights.
Hindley's little son, the heir of the Earnshaws.
notes.n: He is the Hareton whom Lockwood met as a grown, rough young man in Chapters I and II.

notes.g: 'The little master': Joseph's name for Hareton.

notes.t: seek the kitchen and their society
notes.g: Go and sit with them in the kitchen.
The fire in 'the house', the main living room at the Heights.
notes.n: See Chapter I: the farmhouse's big family room is simply called 'the house'.

notes.g: Saved, but only narrowly, like someone pulled from a fire.
notes.n: From the Bible (1 Corinthians 3:15): 'he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire'. Joseph thinks Hindley's sufferings have saved his soul.
'Kirk' is the northern and Scottish word for church.

notes.g: Pushed in and took the page's place.
Before he got drunk enough to lose his reason.
The snap of a scissors-like tool for trimming candle wicks.
notes.n: Candle wicks then didn't burn away neatly, so they had to be trimmed often to stop the candle smoking.

notes.g: Come back from his night-time vigil.
notes.n: Isabella said he went 'straight down to the Grange' every night.

notes.g: A word or look I couldn't hold back.
Heathcliff, who lives at the Heights as Hindley's guest.
notes.n: Heathcliff came to lodge with Hindley in Chapter X.

notes.g: Join forces to pay it off.
notes.n: Hindley talks about revenge as paying off a debt.

notes.g: As weak and mild as Edgar.

notes.t: a retaliation that wouldn’t recoil on myself
notes.g: Revenge that wouldn't come back to hurt me.
Weapons that wound the user as well as the target.

notes.m: 'Dumb' meant not speaking, not stupid.

notes.n: Heathcliff has been winning Hindley's money at cards since Chapter X.

notes.t: it wants three minutes of one
notes.g: It's three minutes to one o'clock.

notes.t: implements which I described to you in my letter
notes.g: Hindley's weapon: a pistol with a spring knife attached.
notes.n: Isabella described this 'curiously-constructed pistol' in her letter in Chapter XIII.

notes.g: Do right by Hareton, his son and heir.

notes.t: trouble your head to screen me

notes.g: The only thing I could do.
A window with small panes set in a criss-cross frame of lead.

notes.t: has a mind to shoot you
too small a stock of hypocrisy
notes.g: Too little hypocrisy (to pretend I cared).
The low, mean attitude I showed.
The window, a glass frame that opens on hinges.
The second person just mentioned: Heathcliff.
The upright iron bars across the window.

notes.m: 'Suffer' here means allow, not feel pain.

notes.g: Gloating in what I thought was safety.

notes.n: A northern and Scottish word.

notes.g: Like the loyal dogs of old stories that pined to death on their masters' graves.

notes.n: A legal phrase for helping someone commit a crime.
The 'charge' is the load of gunpowder and shot in the pistol.

notes.g: Snapped shut into Hindley's own wrist.
notes.n: The spring knife was fixed along the pistol barrel.

notes.g: The stone or wooden upright between two window openings.

notes.m: 'Senseless' here means knocked out, not foolish.

notes.n: 'Flags' are flagstones, large flat paving stones.

notes.g: Onto the long wooden bench with a high back, by the fire.

notes.t: the purport of my hasty tale
notes.g: The meaning of my rushed story.

notes.s: What is ther to do, now?
notes.e: what is ther to do, now?
notes.tr: What's going on now? What's the matter now?

notes.t: I’ll have him to an asylum
notes.g: I'll have him locked up in a madhouse.
notes.n: Asylums for the insane were grim, prison-like places in the 1700s.

notes.g: Old dog without teeth: an insult to Joseph.

notes.t: it is more than half brandy
notes.g: The mess on the floor is mostly spilled brandy, which could catch fire.

notes.s: And so ye’ve been murthering on him?
notes.tr: So you've been murdering him? If ever I saw a sight like this! May the Lord...

notes.t: If iver I seed a seeght loike this
notes.g: If ever I saw a sight like this.

notes.t: malefactors show themselves at the foot of the gallows
notes.g: As criminals sometimes act when about to be hanged.
notes.n: Hangings were public, and some condemned men famously joked or swaggered on the scaffold.

notes.m: 'Directly' meant immediately, not 'in a straight line'.

notes.g: Edgar was a local Justice of the Peace.
notes.n: Magistrates were unpaid local gentlemen who dealt with crimes and disputes in their district. Joseph means to report the attack to him.

notes.t: though he had fifty wives dead
notes.g: Even if he were mourning fifty wives.
Answers forced out of me with difficulty.

notes.m: 'Presently' meant 'shortly', not 'at this moment'.
'Insensible' meant without feeling or awareness, not foolish.

notes.g: The flat stone in front of the fireplace.
His evil spirit; the one who brings him harm (Heathcliff).
notes.n: From the old Roman idea that each person has an attendant spirit, or 'genius'.

notes.m: Dinner was the main meal, eaten around midday. It is just before noon here.

notes.n: The basilisk was a legendary serpent that could kill with a look.
Nelly has in mind the Bible's teaching that revenge belongs to God: 'Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord' (Romans 12:19).

notes.g: Arrogant; taking on what belongs to God.

notes.t: an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth
notes.g: The Old Testament rule of equal payback (Exodus 21:24).
notes.n: In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus rejects it and says to turn the other cheek (Matthew 5:38-39). That is Nelly's point.

notes.g: A whole army of little devils.
notes.n: 'Legion' recalls the demons in the Gospels who say 'My name is Legion: for we are many' (Mark 5:9).

notes.m: Not 'foolish': 'insensible' meant not noticing or feeling.

notes.t: he has murdered one of you
notes.g: She means Catherine, Hindley's sister, whose death she blames on Heathcliff.
His eyes, which she pictures as windows into hell.
notes.n: A twist on the saying that the eyes are the windows of the soul.

notes.t: assumed the ridiculous, contemptible, degrading title of Mrs. Heathcliff
notes.g: Taken the name Mrs. Heathcliff, as Isabella herself did.
notes.n: She means: if Catherine had married Heathcliff instead of Edgar.
Hindley is the 'host' because Heathcliff lives in his house as a guest.

notes.t: bid Joseph speed to his master
notes.g: Told Joseph to hurry to Hindley.

notes.t: hanging a litter of puppies from a chair-back
notes.g: Hareton, a small child, is copying the cruelty around him.
notes.n: Remember Isabella's dog Fanny, found hanging by a handkerchief the night she eloped (Chapter XII).

notes.g: A soul set free from punishment.
notes.n: In Catholic belief, purgatory is a place where souls suffer to be purified before entering heaven.

notes.g: The Grange's lights, shining like a signal fire.
A woman's hat tied under the chin.

notes.t: bestowed a similar salute on me
notes.m: A 'salute' was a kiss or greeting, not a military salute.

notes.g: Isabella's springer spaniel, rescued by Nelly in Chapter XII.

notes.t: a few months subsequent to her escape
notes.g: A few months after her escape.
Isabella named her son Linton, her own family surname.
notes.n: So this boy is Heathcliff's son. From now on 'Linton' can mean this child. Edgar is also often called 'Linton' or 'Mr. Linton', so check which one is meant.

notes.t: it was not of any moment

notes.m: No sexual sense. To 'molest' meant to trouble or annoy.

notes.n: In law a father then had full rights over his children, and a mother had almost none. Heathcliff could claim his son.

notes.t: threw up his office of magistrate
notes.g: Gave up his post as Justice of the Peace.

notes.m: Not overseas. 'Abroad' meant out of doors.

notes.t: pray for Catherine’s soul to haunt him
notes.g: A contrast with Heathcliff, who begged Catherine's ghost to haunt him in Chapter XVI.
In time he came to calm acceptance.

notes.m: Not 'in spite of'. It means paying no attention to.

notes.t: the puny successor to the departed
notes.g: The tiny baby who took her dead mother's place.

notes.n: A sceptre is the rod a king holds as a sign of rule. The baby rules Edgar's heart.

notes.g: The baby is named after her mother.
notes.n: Two Catherines: the mother (born Earnshaw, then Mrs. Linton), now dead, and her daughter Catherine Linton, whom Lockwood met at the Heights in Chapter II. Nelly calls the daughter 'Cathy'.

notes.t: never called the first Catherine short
notes.g: Edgar always called his wife 'Catherine', never 'Cathy'.
When his ship hit the rocks.
notes.n: Nelly's image: in disaster the captain (Hindley) deserted his post, and the crew (his passions) ran riot.

notes.t: they chose their own lots, and were righteously doomed to endure them
notes.g: Each chose his own fate and justly had to live with it.
The local doctor, an old friend of the Earnshaws.

notes.t: an instant presentiment of bad news
notes.g: A sudden feeling that bad news was coming.
Wear black and keep the customs of grief.

notes.t: Who’s given us the slip now
notes.g: Who has slipped away from us? That is, who has died?

notes.t: nip up the corner of your apron
notes.g: Have your apron ready to wipe your tears.

notes.n: Kenneth uses it slyly of Catherine, though she was Edgar's wife: he knows how close she and Heathcliff were.

notes.m: A 'gossip' was a close friend or drinking companion, not someone who spreads rumours.

notes.t: I said we should draw water
notes.g: Probably: I told you we'd be in tears.

notes.n: A common saying; rich gentlemen had a name for hard drinking.
Nelly is the same age. Scholars date Hindley's death to late 1784.

notes.g: Catherine's death. She was Mrs. Linton by marriage.
Had he been treated fairly, or was there foul play?

notes.t: the last duties to the dead
notes.g: Laying out the body and arranging the funeral.
Hindley, whom Nelly grew up with almost as a sister.
notes.n: Nelly's mother nursed Hindley as a baby (Chapter IV).

notes.t: the child Hareton was his wife’s nephew
notes.g: Hareton is Catherine's brother's son, so Edgar is his uncle by marriage.
Take legal charge of the boy and his affairs.
What happened to Hindley's land and money, and what his will said.
Every bit of the land has been pledged as security for loans.
notes.n: If the loans aren't repaid, the lender can take the land.

notes.g: The person who would normally inherit: Hareton.
The heart of the person who is owed the money.

notes.t: buried at the cross-roads, without ceremony
notes.n: Suicides were refused a Christian burial and were traditionally buried at crossroads. England ended the custom in 1823.

notes.tr: I'd rather he had gone for the doctor himself! I'd have taken better care of the master than he did, and he wasn't dead when I left, nothing of the sort!
notes.n: Joseph doubts that Heathcliff did all he could for Hindley.

notes.g: Play the part of a mourner.

notes.m: 'Peculiar' meant particular or special, not strange.

notes.t: one tree won’t grow as crooked as another, with the same wind to twist it
notes.g: Raised the same harsh way, Hareton will turn out as warped as I did.
notes.n: Remember how Hindley treated the boy Heathcliff after old Mr. Earnshaw died (Chapter VI).

notes.m: 'Intimate' here is a verb meaning to hint or make known.

notes.t: supply the place of this with my own
notes.g: Replace this boy with my own son.
notes.n: He means Isabella's baby son.

notes.t: The guest was now the master
notes.g: Heathcliff, once a guest in the house, now owned it.
The lender who holds the mortgage, and so can claim the land.

notes.t: the first gentleman in the neighbourhood
notes.g: The leading landowner of the district.

notes.t: deprived of the advantage of wages
